title: Officer lacked data to prevent shooting: lawyer
article: More information about the violent history of a Sudanese immigrant could have changed the fatal encounter between a lone police officer and Deng Fermino Kuol, a fatality inquiry heard Wednesday.
Better communication with officers in the field is one recommendation heard during the last day of the fatality inquiry before provincial court judge Gerald Meagher.
Const. Ira Macumber was working alone when he shot Kuol twice after being slashed in the arm with a knife on Oct. 25, 2003.
The judge's recommendations will follow in a report to the Attorney General's department.

Lawyer George Blochert, appearing as agent for Kuol's family, said police should have handled the 34-year-old differently. Kuol, who was heavily intoxicated at the time, was unpredictable and irrational under the influence of alcohol, said Blochert.
"They should be treated with the greatest amount of care," he said.

Earlier in the inquiry, Macumber testified he was given no information about the address or the person he was dispatched to check on. Had he known, he would have handled the situation differently, he said.

The final day of the inquiry heard from a Calgary Police Service communications training officer, who told court police computer systems for checking background and identification have been upgraded since the shooting.
Computers now automatically check addresses and names when they are added to the system. The night of the shooting, the 911 operator on duty did not check to see if Kuol had a record.
David Yall, the man who called for help, was mistakenly noted as "Wall," and when he reported the drunken man was called Deng, the call taker recorded it as "Ding."
The 911 call taker should have been able to call up Kuol's checkered past on the local Police Information Management System, or the Canadian Police Information Centre's national database.
The checks would have revealed Kuol's criminal past, which included convictions for assault and drunk driving.
An assault on another police officer four months earlier at the same Forest Lawn address, in the 1700 block of 37th Street S.E., was also not made available to the dispatcher.
A warrant issued 11 days before Kuol's death would also have been available on the police networks.
"Had (Macumber) known about a violent background, he would have acted differently," said Blochert.
Meagher also heard from counsel that 911 callers need to be completely clear when reporting information to dispatchers.
Macumber testified in August that he was helping Kuol up a flight of stairs when the man turned around and tried to stab him in the chest.
The knife bounced off Macumber's body armour and slashed his bicep.
As the two men struggled on the stairs, Macumber was able to pull out his gun and fire two rounds.
Kuol was taken to hospital, where he died a short time later.

Martin Yak, a spokesman for the New Alberta Sudanese Community Association, said the community, which expressed concern and outrage over Kuol's death, is satisfied with the fatality inquiry's thoroughness.
"We'll wait and see what the recommendations are. Otherwise, this is over for us. We have closure," Yak said outside provincial court.
After the inquiry's start on Aug. 8, Yak made a surprise request for legal representation on behalf of Kuol's sister, who is in Australia.
Blochert said Kuol was seeking a better life in Canada after leaving war-torn Sudan.
"It is a sad irony that he is shot by a police officer," he said.
"This is not the Canadian way of doing things."
Meagher will provide a written report outlining the facts and circumstances of the case and his recommendations.
